children.text: kiṃvā rasavikalpāc ca tathā doṣavikalpāc ca hetvādijñānaṃ pṛthageva vaktavyaṃ rasabhedāddhi tatkāryaṃ liṅgamapi jñāyate hetubheṣajavijñānaṃ tu // 5
children.translated_text: Or, the knowledge of causes etc. should be stated separately from <s>rasa</s>-varieties and <s>doṣa</s>-varieties: for from the distinction of <s>rasas</s>, the symptoms which are their effects are also known; and the knowledge of causes and medicines // 5

children.text: rasabhedavijñānādeva vaktavyaṃ yato rasabhedavad dravyameva vikārāṇāṃ heturbheṣajaṃ ca bhavatīti evaṃ doṣabhedaṃ jñātvā ca tasya samānaṃ hetuṃ pratyeti doṣavirodhi ca dravyaṃ bheṣajamiti // 6
children.translated_text: should be stated as [deriving] from <s>rasa</s>-distinction alone, since a substance possessing distinct <s>rasas</s> is both the cause of diseases and the medicine. Thus, having known <s>doṣa</s>-distinction, one infers the cause similar to it, and the substance antagonistic to the <s>doṣa</s> is the medicine. // 6

children.text: tad yuktam uktaṃ na sa muhyedvikārāṇāṃ hetuliṅgopaśāntiṣviti // 7]
children.translated_text: Therefore it is well said: 'He is not confused regarding the causes, symptoms, and treatments of diseases.' // 7]

children.text: vyaktaḥ śuṣkasya cādau ca raso dravyasya lakṣyate /
children.translated_text: The <s>rasa</s> (taste) of a substance is perceived manifestly — whether dry, and initially;

children.text: viparyayeṇānuraso raso nāsti hi saptamaḥ // Car_1,26.28
children.translated_text: the contrary is <s>anurasa</s> (secondary taste) — there is no seventh <s>rasa</s>. // Car 1.26.28
[{<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s>}
He states the definition of <s>rasa</s> and <s>anurasa</s> mentioned earlier: 'manifest' etc. // 1

children.text: śuṣkasya ceti cakārād ārdrasya ca ādau ceti cakārādante ca tena śuṣkasya vārdrasya vā prathamajihvāsambandhe vāsvādānte vā yo vyaktatvena madhuro 'yam amlo 'yam ityādinā vikalpena gṛhyate sa vyaktaḥ yas tūktāvasthācatuṣṭaye 'pi vyakto nopalabhyate kiṃ tarhy avyapadeśyatayā chāyāmātreṇa kāryadarśanena vā mīyate so 'nurasa iti vākyārthaḥ // 2
children.translated_text: The word 'ca' in 'of the dry and' includes 'of the moist also'; 'ca' in 'initially and' includes 'at the end also.' Therefore, whether of a dry or moist [substance], whether at the first contact with the tongue or at the end of tasting, that which is apprehended manifestly through discrimination as 'this is sweet, this is sour' etc. — that is the manifest [<s>rasa</s>]. But that which, even in all four stated conditions, is not manifestly perceived, but rather is inferred only through a mere trace, being undefinable, or through observing its effects — that is the <s>anurasa</s> (secondary taste). This is the meaning of the passage. // 2

children.text: yataśca madhurādaya eva vyaktatvāvyaktatvābhyāṃ rasānurasarūpāḥ ato'vyakto nāma saptamo raso nāsti // 3
children.translated_text: And since the sweet etc. themselves, through manifestness and non-manifestness, take the form of <s>rasa</s> and <s>anurasa</s>, therefore there is no seventh <s>rasa</s> called 'non-manifest.' // 3

children.text: ayaṃ cārthaḥ pūrvaṃ pratiṣiddho 'pyanuguṇaspaṣṭahetuprāptyā punar niṣidhyate // 4
children.translated_text: And this meaning, though refuted earlier, is refuted again due to the obtaining of a consistent and clear reason. // 4

children.text: anye tv āhuḥ śuṣkasya cetyanena yasya dravyasya śuṣkasya cārdrasya copayogaḥ tatra śuṣkāvasthāyāṃ yo 'vyaktaḥ sa rasa ucyate yastvārdrāvasthāyāṃ vyaktaḥ san śuṣkāvasthāyāṃ nānuyāti nāsau rasaḥ kiṃtv anurasaḥ // 5
children.translated_text: Others, however, say: by 'of the dry and' — for a substance that is used both in dry and moist states, in the dry state that which is manifest is called the <s>rasa</s>; but that which is manifest in the moist state but does not persist in the dry state — that is not a <s>rasa</s> but an <s>anurasa</s>. // 5

children.text: yathā pippalyā ārdrāyā madhuro raso vyaktaḥ śuṣkāyāstu pippalyāḥ kaṭukaḥ tena kaṭuka eva rasaḥ pippalyāḥ madhurastvanurasaḥ yastu drākṣādīnām ārdrāvasthāyāṃ śuṣkāvasthāyāṃ ca madhura eva tatra vipratipattirapi nāsti tena tatra madhura eva rasaḥ nityārdraprayojyānāṃ tu kāñjikatakrādīnāmādau vyakto ya upalabhyate rasaḥ anu copalabhyate yaḥ so 'nuraso yuktas tiktatvādiḥ tathā ārdrāvasthāyāṃ śuṣkāvasthāviparīto yaḥ pippalyā iva madhuraḥ so 'nurasa iti // 6
children.translated_text: For example, in moist long pepper, the sweet taste is manifest; but in dry long pepper, pungent [is manifest]. Therefore pungent alone is the <s>rasa</s> of long pepper; sweet is the <s>anurasa</s>. But for grapes and such, which are sweet in both moist and dry states, there is no disagreement — sweet is simply the <s>rasa</s>. For those always used moist, like <s>kāñjika</s> (fermented gruel) and <s>takra</s> (buttermilk), that which is perceived manifestly at first is the <s>rasa</s>, and that perceived subsequently is the <s>anurasa</s> — such as bitterness etc. Likewise, in the moist state, that which is contrary to the dry state — like the sweetness of long pepper — is the <s>anurasa</s>. // 6

children.text: kiṃtv ārdrāpi pippalī madhurarasaiveti paśyāmaḥ yato vakṣyati śleṣmalā madhurā cārdrā gurvī snigdhā ca pippalī iti madhurasya tatrānurasatve gurutvaśleṣmakartṛtvāny anupapannāni tena ārdrā pippalī vyaktamadhurarasaiva śuṣkā tu madhurānuraseti yuktam // 7]
children.translated_text: However, we consider that even moist long pepper is indeed of sweet <s>rasa</s>, since [the text] will state: 'Moist long pepper is <s>śleṣma</s>-producing, sweet, heavy, and unctuous.' If sweet were merely an <s>anurasa</s> there, the heaviness and <s>śleṣma</s>-producing properties would be unexplained. Therefore, moist long pepper is indeed of manifest sweet <s>rasa</s>, while dry [long pepper] has sweet as <s>anurasa</s> — this is proper. // 7]

children.text: parāparatve yuktiśca saṃkhyā saṃyoga eva ca /
children.translated_text: Superiority and inferiority, rational planning, number, combination,

children.text: vibhāgaśca pṛthaktvaṃ ca parimāṇamathāpi ca // Car_1,26.29
children.translated_text: separation, distinctness, and also measure — // Car 1.26.29
processing, and habituation — these are the qualities to be known, beginning with 'superiority' etc.;
[they are] the means of accomplishment in therapeutics — we shall describe them by their definitions. // Car 1.26.30
With regard to region, time, age, measure, digestion, potency, taste, and such —

children.text: parāparatve yuktiśca yojanā yā tu yujyate // Car_1,26.31
children.translated_text: superiority and inferiority, and rational planning, is that combination which is proper. // Car 1.26.31

children.text: saṃkhyā syādgaṇitaṃ yogaḥ saha saṃyoga ucyate /
children.translated_text: Number is enumeration; combination is said to be the joining together
of substances — [it is] produced by the action of two, all, or one, and is always impermanent. // Car 1.26.32
Separation is division — disjunction, or grasping in parts;
distinctness is non-conjunction, dissimilarity, and plurality. // Car 1.26.33
Measure, moreover, is quantification; processing is considered to be transformation;
habituation is the repeated practice of a substance — regular practice, constant action. // Car 1.26.34
Thus, by their individual characteristics, all the qualities beginning with superiority etc. have been stated —

children.text: cikitsā yair aviditair na yathāvat pravartate // Car_1,26.35
children.translated_text: [those] without knowledge of which, therapeutics does not proceed properly. // Car 1.26.35
[{<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s>}

children.text: samprati pūrvoktagurvādiguṇātiriktān paratvāparatvādīn daśa guṇān rasadharmatvenopadeṣṭavyānāha paretyādi // 1
children.translated_text: Now he states ten qualities — superiority, inferiority, etc. — beyond the previously mentioned heaviness etc. qualities, which are to be taught as properties of <s>rasa</s>: 'superiority' etc. // 1
And superiority (<s>paratva</s>) means pre-eminence; inferiority (<s>aparatva</s>) means non-pre-eminence. // 2
The elaboration of this is 'region, time' etc. // 3

children.text: tatra deśo maruḥ paraḥ anūpo 'paraḥ kālo visargaḥ paraḥ ādānamaparaḥ vayastaruṇaṃ param aparam itaran mānaṃ ca śarīrasya yathā vakṣyamāṇaṃ śarīre paraṃ tato'nyadaparaṃ pākavīryarasāstu ye yasya yoginaste taṃ prati parāḥ ayaugikās tv aparāḥ // 4
children.translated_text: There: the desert region is superior; the marshy land is inferior. The <s>visarga</s> (cool) season is superior; the <s>ādāna</s> (hot) season is inferior. Youth is superior; other [ages] are inferior. And the measure of the body — as will be stated regarding the body — is superior; other than that is inferior. Digestion, potency, and <s>rasas</s> that are suited to a particular [case] are superior with respect to it; those that are unsuited are inferior. // 4
By the word 'etc.' (<s>ādi</s>), constitution (<s>prakṛti</s>), strength (<s>bala</s>), and such are included. // 5

children.text: kiṃvā paratvāparatve vaiśeṣikokte jñeye tatra deśāpekṣayā saṃnikṛṣṭadeśasambandhinam apekṣya vidūradeśasambandhini paratvaṃ saṃnikṛṣṭadeśasambandhini cāparatvaṃ bhavati evaṃ saṃnikṛṣṭaviprakṛṣṭakālāpekṣayā ca sthavire paratvaṃ yūni cāparatvaṃ bhavati // 6
children.translated_text: Or, superiority and inferiority as taught by the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> [school] should be known: there, with respect to region, in relation to one connected with a near region, superiority belongs to one connected with a distant region, and inferiority to one connected with a near region. Likewise, with respect to near and distant time, superiority belongs to the old and inferiority to the young. // 6

children.text: vayaḥprabhṛtiṣu paratvāparatvaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ kāladeśakṛtam evehopayogād upacaritam apyabhihitaṃ yato na guṇe mānādau guṇāntarasambhavaḥ // 7
children.translated_text: In age and the rest, superiority and inferiority are, as applicable, caused by time and region alone. [Their attribution] to these is figurative due to practical utility here, since a quality like 'measure' etc. cannot possess another quality. // 7

children.text: yuktiścetyādau yojanā doṣādyapekṣayā bheṣajasya samīcīnakalpanā ata evoktaṃ yā tu yujyate yā kalpanā yaugikī bhavati sā tu yuktir ucyate ayaugikī tu kalpanāpi satī yuktir nocyate putro 'pyaputravat // 8
children.translated_text: In 'and rational planning' etc.: 'combination' (<s>yojanā</s>) is the proper formulation of medicine with reference to <s>doṣas</s> etc. Therefore it is said 'which is proper' — meaning: that formulation which is appropriate is called <s>yukti</s> (rational planning); a formulation which, even though existent, is not appropriate is not called <s>yukti</s> — like a son who is [treated as] sonless. // 8
And this <s>yukti</s>, though included within combination, measure, processing, etc., is stated separately because of its extreme usefulness. // 9
He defines number: 'number' etc. // 10
'Enumeration' here means one, two, three, etc. // 11
He states combination: 'joining' etc. // 12

children.text: saheti militānāṃ dravyāṇāṃ yogaḥ prāptirityarthaḥ sahetyanenehākiṃcitkaraṃ parasparasaṃyogaṃ nirākaroti // 13
children.translated_text: 'Together' means the meeting or coming together of mixed substances. By [the word] 'together,' he excludes a mere mutual contact that produces no effect. // 13
He states its varieties: 'of two' etc. // 14

children.text: tatra dvaṃdvakarmajo yathā yudhyamānayor meṣayoḥ sarvakarmajo yathā bhāṇḍe prakṣipyamāṇānāṃ māṣāṇāṃ bahulamāṣakriyā yogajaḥ ekakarmajo yathā vṛkṣavāyasayoḥ // 15
children.translated_text: There: produced by the action of two — as in two fighting rams; produced by the action of all — as in the mixing of many beans thrown into a vessel; produced by the action of one — as in the [conjunction of] a tree and a crow. // 15
'Impermanent' shows that combination, being produced by action, is impermanent. // 16
He states separation: 'separation indeed' etc. // 17
'Division' means the act of dividing. // 18

children.text: vibhaktimeva vivṛṇoti viyoga iti saṃyogasya vigamo viyogaḥ // 19
children.translated_text: He elaborates on division: 'disjunction' — the departure of conjunction is disjunction. // 19

children.text: tat kiṃ saṃyogābhāva eva viyoga ityāha bhāgaśo graha iti // 20
children.translated_text: Is disjunction then merely the absence of conjunction? He answers: 'grasping in parts.' // 20

children.text: vibhāgaśo vibhaktatvena grahaṇaṃ yato bhavatīti bhāvaḥ tena vibhaktirityeṣā bhāvarūpā pratītir na saṃyogābhāvamātraṃ bhavati kiṃtarhi bhāvarūpavibhāgaguṇayuktā ityarthaḥ // 21
children.translated_text: The sense is: because apprehension occurs in a divided manner, i.e., as separated. Therefore this 'division' is a positive cognition, not merely the absence of conjunction — rather, it is [a cognition] possessing the positive quality of separation. // 21

children.text: pṛthaktvaṃ tu idaṃ dravyaṃ paṭalakṣaṇaṃ ghaṭāt pṛthag ityādikā buddhiryato bhavati tat pṛthaktvaṃ bhavati // 22
children.translated_text: Distinctness (<s>pṛthaktva</s>), however, is: that [quality] due to which the cognition arises — 'this substance characterized as cloth is distinct from a pot' — that is distinctness. // 22
And the teacher states this in three varieties: 'distinctness' etc. // 23

children.text: tatra yat sarvathāsaṃyujyamānayoriva meruhimācalayoḥ pṛthaktvam etadasaṃyoga ityanenoktam // 24
children.translated_text: There: that distinctness which is of things absolutely never conjoined — like Mount <s>Meru</s> and the <s>Himālayas</s> — this is stated by 'non-conjunction.' // 24

children.text: tathā saṃyujyamānānāmapi pṛthaktvaṃ vijātīyānāṃ mahiṣavarāhādīnāṃ tadāha vailakṣaṇyamityādi // 25
children.translated_text: Likewise, the distinctness even of things [capable of being] conjoined, when they are of different classes — like buffaloes and boars — is stated by 'dissimilarity' etc. // 25
The meaning is: the distinctness of things of different classes, characterized by possessing distinctive features. // 26

children.text: tathaikajātīyānāmapy avilakṣaṇānāṃ māṣāṇāṃ pṛthaktvaṃ bhavatītyāha anekateti // 27
children.translated_text: Likewise, even among things of the same class that are not dissimilar — like [individual] beans — distinctness exists. This is stated by 'plurality.' // 27

children.text: ekajātīyeṣu hi saṃyukteṣu na vailakṣaṇyaṃ nāpyasaṃyogaḥ atha cānekatā pṛthaktvarūpā bhavatīti bhāvaḥ // 28
children.translated_text: For among things of the same class that are conjoined, there is neither dissimilarity nor non-conjunction; yet plurality, which is a form of distinctness, exists. This is the sense. // 28

children.text: kiṃvā pṛthaktvaṃ guṇāntaramicchan lokavyavahārārtham asaṃyogavailakṣaṇyānekatārūpameva yathodāhṛtaṃ pṛthaktvaṃ darśayati // 29
children.translated_text: Or, wishing [to explain] distinctness as a separate quality, he shows, for the purpose of worldly usage, that distinctness takes the forms of non-conjunction, dissimilarity, and plurality, as illustrated. // 29
Measure is what is measurable by <s>prastha</s>, <s>āḍhaka</s>, scales, and such. //

children.text: karaṇaṃ guṇāntarādhāyakatvaṃ saṃskaraṇamityarthaḥ yadvakṣyati saṃskāro hi guṇāntarādhānamucyate iti // 30
children.translated_text: 'Transformation' means the capacity to impart a different quality — i.e., processing. As will be stated: 'Processing is said to be the imparting of a different quality.' // 30
Habituation is the repeated practice of [foods like] <s>���aṣṭika</s> rice, of exercises, etc. // 31

children.text: abhyasanameva lokaprasiddhābhyāṃ paryāyābhyāṃ vivṛṇoti śīlanaṃ satatakriyeti yaṃ lokāḥ śīlanasatatakriyābhyām abhidadhati so 'bhyāsa iti bhāvaḥ // 32
children.translated_text: He elaborates 'repeated practice' with two popular synonyms: 'regular practice' and 'constant action' — meaning: what people denote by 'regular practice' and 'constant action' is <s>abhyāsa</s> (habituation). // 32

children.text: ayaṃ ca saṃyogasaṃskāraviśeṣarūpo 'pi viśeṣeṇa cikitsopayuktatvāt pṛthagucyate // 33
children.translated_text: And this [habituation], though a form of a particular kind of combination and processing, is stated separately because it is especially useful in therapeutics. // 33

children.text: na yathāvat pravartata iti vacanena śabdādiṣu ca gurvādiṣu ca parādīnāmaprādhānyaṃ sūcayati // 34]
children.translated_text: By the statement 'does not proceed properly,' he indicates that the superiority etc. qualities are subordinate to the [primary qualities like] sound etc. and heaviness etc. // 34]
Qualities [do not reside] in qualities — [this has been] stated; therefore let the physician
know the qualities stated regarding <s>rasas</s> as qualities of substances — the author's intentions are of various kinds. // Car 1.26.36
[{<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s>}

children.text: samprati rasānāṃ parasparasaṃyogo guṇa uktaḥ tathāgre ca snigdhatvādirguṇo vācyaḥ sa ca guṇarūparase na sambhavatīti yathā rasānāṃ guṇanirdeśo boddhavyas tadāha guṇā ityādi // 1
children.translated_text: Now, the mutual combination of <s>rasas</s> has been stated as a quality; and hereafter, unctuousness etc. will be stated as qualities — but these cannot exist in <s>rasa</s> which is itself a quality. Therefore he explains how the attribution of qualities to <s>rasas</s> should be understood: 'qualities' etc. // 1

children.text: guṇā guṇāśrayā noktā iti dīrghaṃjīvitīye samavāyī tu niśceṣṭaḥ kāraṇaṃ guṇaḥ ityanena // 2
children.translated_text: 'Qualities [do not reside] in qualities — [this has been] stated' — [it was stated] in the <s>Dīrghaṃjīvitīya</s> [chapter] by: 'that which inheres, is inactive, and is a cause — that is a quality.' // 2

children.text: rasaguṇāniti rase snigdhādīn guṇān nirdiṣṭān tad rasādhāradravyaguṇān eva vidyāt // 3
children.translated_text: 'Qualities of <s>rasas</s>' means: the qualities such as unctuousness etc. attributed to <s>rasas</s> should be known as qualities of the substances that are the substrata of those <s>rasas</s>. // 3

children.text: nanu yadi dravyaguṇā eva te tat kimiti rasaguṇatvenocyanta ityāha karturityādi karturiti tantrakartuḥ // 4
children.translated_text: Objection: If they are indeed qualities of substances, then why are they called qualities of <s>rasas</s>? He answers: 'of the author' etc. — 'of the author' means of the composer of the treatise. // 4

children.text: abhiprāyā iti tatra tatropacāreṇa tathā sāmānyaśabdādiprayogeṇa tantrakaraṇabuddhayaḥ sāmānyaśabdopacārādiprayogaś ca prakaraṇādivaśād eva sphuṭatvāt tathā prayojanavaśāc ca kriyate // 5
children.translated_text: 'Intentions' — there, through secondary usage (<s>upacāra</s>) in various contexts, and through the use of general terms and the like, the intentions of the treatise-maker [are expressed]. The use of general terms, secondary usage, and the like is done precisely because of the clarity provided by the context (<s>prakaraṇa</s>) and the like, and also because of the purpose [intended]. // 5

children.text: tacca prakaraṇādi ataśca prakṛtaṃ buddhvā ityādau darśayiṣyāmaḥ // 6
children.translated_text: And that context and the like — we shall demonstrate in 'therefore, having understood what is being discussed' and so on. // 6

children.text: iha ca dravyaguṇānāṃ raseṣu yadupacaraṇaṃ tasyāyamabhiprāyo yat madhurādinirdeśenaiva snigdhaśītādiguṇā api prāyo madhurādyavyabhicāriṇo dravye nirdiṣṭā bhavantīti na madhuratvaṃ nirdiśya snigdhatvādipratipādanaṃ punaḥ pṛthak kriyata iti // 7]
children.translated_text: Here, regarding the attribution (<s>upacaraṇa</s>) of the qualities of substances to the tastes — the intention is this: by indicating 'sweet' etc. alone, the qualities such as unctuousness, coldness, etc. — which generally do not deviate from sweet etc. — are also indicated in the substance. Thus, having stated sweetness, the unctuousness and the like need not be separately taught again. // 7]
Therefore, having understood what is being discussed, and the differences of place and time,
and the intentions and methods of the treatise-maker, one should ascertain the meaning. // Car_1,26.37
[<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s> commentary:]

children.text: abhiprāyapṛthaktve sati yathā grantho boddhavyas tadāha ataś cetyādi // 1
children.translated_text: Given that the intentions are distinct, he states how the text should be understood with 'therefore' and so on. // 1

children.text: tatra prakṛtaṃ buddhvā yathā kṣārāḥ kṣīraṃ phalaṃ puṣpam ityatrodbhidagaṇasya prakṛtatvāt kṣīramiti snuhyādikṣīram eva kṣīraśabdena vadet // 2
children.translated_text: 'Having understood what is being discussed' — for example, in [the list] 'alkalis, milk, fruit, flower,' since the class of plants is the subject being discussed, 'milk' (<s>kṣīra</s>) refers by that word to the milk [latex] of <s>Snuhī</s> (Euphorbia) and the like alone. // 2

children.text: deśāntaraṃ buddhveti yathā śirasi śodhane 'bhidhīyamāne krimivyādhau iti tacchirogatakrimivyādhāv eva bhavati // 3
children.translated_text: 'Having understood the difference of place' — for example, when purification of the head is being discussed, '[remedy] for worm-disease' refers only to the worm-disease located in the head. // 3

children.text: kālāntare yathā vamanakāle 'bhihitaṃ pratigrahāṃś copahārayed iti tatra pratigrahaśabdena pātramucyate na tu grahaṇaṃ pratigrahaḥ // 4
children.translated_text: 'Difference of time' — for example, what is stated at the time of emesis: 'one should bring forth receptacles' — there, by the word 'receptacle' (<s>pratigraha</s>), a vessel is meant, not [the act of] receiving. // 4

children.text: tantrakartur abhiprāyān iti yathoktaṃ raseṣu guṇāropaṇe tad boddhavyam // 5
children.translated_text: 'The intentions of the treatise-maker' — for example, what was stated regarding the attribution of qualities to tastes — that should be understood [as his intention]. // 5
'Methods' (<s>upāya</s>) means the methods of the treatise — i.e., the <s>tantrayukti</s> (hermeneutic devices). // 6
'Meaning' (<s>artha</s>) means what is signified. // 7

children.text: yadyapi prakṛtādayo 'pi tantrakartur abhiprāyā eva tathāpi yatra prakṛtatvādi na sphuṭaṃ pratīyate tatra tantrakartur abhiprāyatvena boddhavyam // 8]
children.translated_text: Although 'what is being discussed' and the like are themselves intentions of the treatise-maker, nevertheless, where the fact of [something] being the topic under discussion is not clearly apparent, it should be understood as [simply] the intention of the treatise-maker. // 8]
I shall now declare, hereafter, the six divisions of the tastes —

children.text: ṣaṭ pañcabhūtaprabhavāḥ saṃkhyātāśca yathā rasāḥ // Car_1,26.38
children.translated_text: how the six tastes, originating from the five elements, are enumerated. // Car_1,26.38
[<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s> commentary:]
'Six divisions' means the six categories beginning with sweet and so on. // 1

children.text: ṣaṭ pañcabhūtaprabhavā iti pañcabhūtaprabhavāḥ santo yathoktena prakāreṇa somaguṇātirekāt ityādinā yathā ṣaṭ saṃkhyātāḥ ṣaṭsaṃkhyāparicchinnā bhavanti tathā vakṣyāmīti yojanā // 2]
children.translated_text: 'Six, originating from the five elements' — being born of the five elements, how they are enumerated as six — i.e., delimited to the number six — by the stated method, namely 'due to the preponderance of the qualities of <s>Soma</s> (Moon/water)' and so on — 'I shall declare' — this is the construction. // 2]

children.text: saumyāḥ khalvāpo'ntarikṣaprabhavāḥ prakṛtiśītā laghvyaś cāvyaktarasāśca tāstvantarikṣādbhraśyamānā bhraṣṭāśca pañcamahāguṇasamanvitā jaṅgamasthāvarāṇāṃ bhūtānāṃ mūrtīr abhiprīṇayanti tāsu mūrtiṣu ṣaḍ abhimūrchanti rasāḥ // Car_1,26.39
children.translated_text: Waters are lunar (<s>saumya</s>) in nature, originating from the atmosphere, naturally cold, light, and of unmanifest taste. But those [waters], as they fall from the atmosphere, and after having fallen, become endowed with the five great qualities and nourish the forms of living beings — both mobile and immobile. In those forms, the six tastes mature. // Car_1,26.39
[<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s> commentary:]

children.text: samprati rasānām ādikāraṇameva tāvad āha saumyā ityādi // 1
children.translated_text: Now he first states the primary cause of the tastes with 'lunar' and so on. // 1
'Lunar' (<s>saumya</s>) means having <s>Soma</s> (Moon/water) as their presiding deity. // 2

children.text: bhraśyamānā iti vadatā bhūmisambandhavyatirekeṇāntarīkṣeritaiḥ pṛthivyādiparamāṇvādibhiḥ sambandho rasārambhako bhavatīti darśyate // 3
children.translated_text: By saying 'as they fall,' [the author] shows that the contact with atoms of earth and the like — sent forth by the atmosphere, distinct from contact with the earth — is what initiates the tastes. // 3
'Forms' (<s>mūrti</s>) means manifest individual beings. // 4
'Nourish' (<s>abhiprīṇayanti</s>) means satiate; or alternatively, generate. // 5
'The tastes mature' means they come into manifestation. // 6

children.text: atra cāntarīkṣamudakaṃ rasakāraṇatve pradhānatvāduktaṃ tena kṣitistham api sthāvarajaṅgamotpattau rasakāraṇaṃ bhavatyeva // 7]
children.translated_text: Here, atmospheric water is stated [as the cause] because of its primacy in causing taste. By this, earth-based [water] too is indeed a cause of taste in the production of mobile and immobile beings. // 7]

children.text: teṣāṃ ṣaṇṇāṃ rasānāṃ somaguṇātirekānmadhuro rasaḥ pṛthivyagnibhūyiṣṭhatvādamlaḥ salilāgnibhūyiṣṭhatvāl lavaṇaḥ vāyvagnibhūyiṣṭhatvātkaṭukaḥ vāyvākāśātiriktatvāt tiktaḥ pavanapṛthivīvyatirekāt kaṣāya iti /
children.translated_text: Of those six tastes: the sweet taste [arises] from the preponderance of the qualities of <s>Soma</s> (water); the sour from the predominance of earth and fire; the salty from the predominance of water and fire; the pungent from the predominance of wind and fire; the bitter from the excess of wind and space; the astringent from the excess of wind and earth.

children.text: evameṣāṃ rasānāṃ ṣaṭtvam upapannaṃ nyūnātirekaviśeṣān mahābhūtānāṃ bhūtānāmiva sthāvarajaṅgamānāṃ nānāvarṇākṛtiviśeṣāḥ ṣaḍṛtukatvācca kālasyopapanno mahābhūtānāṃ nyūnātirekaviśeṣaḥ // Car_1,26.40
children.translated_text: Thus the sixfold nature of these tastes is established from the specific variations of deficiency and excess of the great elements — just as the various differences of color and form among mobile and immobile beings [arise from such variations]. And the specific variation of deficiency and excess of the great elements is established because time has six seasons. // Car_1,26.40
[<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s> commentary:]

children.text: somaguṇātirekāditi atirekaśabdena sarveṣveva raseṣu sarvabhūtasāṃnidhyam asti kvacit tu kasyacid bhūtaguṇasyātirekād rasaviśeṣe bhavatīti darśayati etacca madhuraṃ prati abguṇātiriktatvaṃ viśeṣotpattau kāraṇatvena jñeyaṃ yaccādhārakāraṇatvam apāṃ tat sarvasādhāraṇam // 1
children.translated_text: 'From the preponderance of the qualities of <s>Soma</s>' — by the word 'preponderance' [the author] shows that in all tastes, all elements are present; but in a particular [taste], a specific taste-variety arises due to the preponderance of a particular element's quality. And this preponderance of water-quality with respect to the sweet [taste] should be understood as a causal factor (<s>nimittakāraṇa</s>) in the production of the specific [taste]. The causality of water as a substrate (<s>ādhārakāraṇa</s>) is common to all [tastes]. // 1
Similarly, the causality of water in the salty [taste] should be understood. // 2

children.text: lavaṇastu suśrute pṛthivyagnyatirekāt paṭhitaḥ asmiṃś ca virodhe kāryavirodho nāstyeva // 3
children.translated_text: The salty [taste] is read in <s>Suśruta</s> as [arising] from the preponderance of earth and fire. There is no contradiction in effect between these [two readings]. // 3

children.text: nanu uṣṇaśītābhyāmagnisalilābhyāṃ kṛtasya lavaṇasyāpy uṣṇaśītatvena bhavitavyaṃ tal lavaṇaṃ katham uṣṇaṃ bhavati naivaṃ yato bhūtānām ayaṃ svabhāvo yat kenacit prakāreṇa saṃniviṣṭāḥ kaṃcid guṇam ārabhante na sarvam // 4
children.translated_text: Objection: Since the salty is produced by fire and water — hot and cold — the salty should also be both hot and cold. How then is the salty hot? [Reply:] It is not so, because this is the nature of the elements — that when arranged in a certain manner, they produce a certain quality, not all [possible qualities]. // 4

children.text: yathā makuṣṭhake 'dbhir madhuro rasaḥ kriyate na snehaḥ tathā saindhave vahnināpi noṣṇatvam ārabhyate // 5
children.translated_text: Just as in <s>Mudga</s> (green gram), water produces the sweet taste but not unctuousness — similarly in rock-salt, even fire does not produce heat. // 5

children.text: ayaṃ ca bhūtānāṃ saṃniveśo 'dṛṣṭaprabhāvakṛta eva sa ca saṃniveśaḥ kāryadarśanenonneyaḥ // 6
children.translated_text: And this arrangement of elements is produced by unseen potency (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>); and that arrangement is to be inferred from the observation of effects. // 6

children.text: tena yatra kāryaṃ dṛśyate tatra kalpyate yathā lavaṇe uṣṇatvād agnir viṣyanditvācca jalamanumīyate // 7
children.translated_text: Therefore, where an effect is seen, there [the element] is postulated — just as in salt, fire is inferred from its hotness, and water from its liquefying property. // 7
And this matter is knowable through authoritative tradition — the speculations of people like us do not extend here. // 8

children.text: etena yaducyate toyavat pṛthivyādayo'pi kimiti pṛthagrasāntaraṃ na kurvanti tathā toyavātādisaṃyogādibhyaḥ kimiti rasāntarāṇi notpadyanta iti tadapi bhūtasvabhāvāparyanuyogād eva pratyuktam // 9
children.translated_text: By this, the [objection] that is raised — 'Why do earth and the other [elements], like water, not individually produce other tastes? And why do tastes not arise from the combination of water with wind and the like?' — that too is answered by [the principle that] the nature of elements is not subject to further inquiry. // 9

children.text: iha ca kāraṇatvaṃ bhūtānāṃ rasasya madhuratvādiviśeṣa eva nimittakāraṇarūpam ucyate tena nīrasānām api hi dahanādīnāṃ kāraṇatvamupapannam eva vyutpāditam // 10
children.translated_text: Here, the causality of elements with respect to taste is stated as efficient cause (<s>nimittakāraṇa</s>) only with respect to the specific varieties such as sweetness etc. Therefore, even the causality of tasteless [elements] like fire and the rest is well-established and has been explained. // 10
Establishing the differentiation of tastes by an example, he says 'Thus' and so on. // 11

children.text: rasānāṃ ṣaṭtvaṃ mahābhūtānāṃ nyūnātirekaviśeṣāt somaguṇātirekapṛthivyagnyatirekādeḥ ṣaḍutpādakāraṇādupapannaṃ ṣaḍbhyaḥ kāraṇebhyaḥ ṣaṭ kāryāṇi bhavantīti yuktameveti bhāvaḥ // 12
children.translated_text: The sixfold nature of tastes is established from the six productive causes — the specific variations of deficiency and excess of the great elements, [namely] preponderance of the quality of <s>Soma</s>, preponderance of earth and fire, and so on. From six causes, six effects arise — this is reasonable — such is the purport. // 12

children.text: bhūtānāṃ yathā nānāvarṇākṛtiviśeṣā mahābhūtānāṃ nyūnātirekaviśeṣāt tathā rasānām apīti // 13
children.translated_text: Just as the various differences of color and form among beings [arise] from the specific variations of deficiency and excess of the great elements — so too for the tastes. // 13

children.text: bhūtānāṃ yathoktānām atirekaviśeṣahetum āha ṣaḍṛtukatvād ityādi // 14
children.translated_text: He states the cause of the specific variations of excess among the aforementioned elements with 'because time has six seasons' and so on. // 14

children.text: ṣaḍṛtukatvena kālo nānāhemantādirūpatayā kaṃcidbhūtaviśeṣaṃ kvacidvardhayati sa cātmakāryaṃ rasaṃ puṣṭaṃ karoti yathā hemantakāle somaguṇātireko bhavati śiśire vāyvākāśātirekaḥ evaṃ tasyāśitīyoktarasotpādakrameṇa vasantādāv api bhūtotkarṣo jñeyaḥ ṣaḍṛtukācceti cakāreṇāhorātrakṛto 'pi bhūtotkarṣo jñeyaḥ tathādṛṣṭakṛtaś ca tena hemantādāv api rasāntarotpādaḥ kvacidvastuny upapanno bhavati // 15
children.translated_text: Because of the six-season nature [of time], time — in its various forms as winter etc. — increases a particular element-predominance somewhere. And that [element] nourishes the taste that is its own effect. For example: in the winter season, there is a preponderance of the qualities of <s>Soma</s>; in the cold season (<s>śiśira</s>), a preponderance of wind and space. Similarly, by the sequence of taste-production stated in the <s>Āśitīya</s> [chapter], the predominance of elements in spring and the like should also be known. The conjunctive particle 'ca' in 'because of six seasons' indicates that the predominance of elements produced by the day-night [cycle] should also be understood — as well as that produced by unseen [karmic] potency. Therefore, the production of other tastes even in winter etc. is possible in certain substances. // 15

children.text: yadyapi ca ṛtubhede'pi bhūtotkarṣaviśeṣa eva kāraṇaṃ yaduktaṃ tāv etāv arkavāyū ityādi tathāpi bījāṅkurakāryakāraṇabhāvavat saṃsārānāditayaiva bhūtaviśeṣartvoḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvo vācyaḥ // 16]
children.translated_text: Although even in the differentiation of seasons, it is specifically the predominance of elements that is the cause — as stated in 'those two, sun and wind' and so on — nevertheless, like the causal relation between seed and sprout, the causal relation between element-predominance and season is to be stated as beginningless due to the beginninglessness of <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclic existence). // 16]

children.text: tatrāgnimārutātmakā rasāḥ prāyeṇordhvabhājaḥ lāghavādutplavanatvāc ca vāyorūrdhvajvalanatvācca vahneḥ salilapṛthivyātmakāstu prāyeṇādhobhājaḥ pṛthivyā gurutvān nimnagatvāc codakasya vyāmiśrātmakāḥ punar ubhayatobhājaḥ // Car_1,26.41
children.translated_text: Among these, tastes that are of the nature of fire and wind are predominantly upward-moving — because of the lightness and upward-floating nature of wind, and because of the upward-burning nature of fire. But those of the nature of water and earth are predominantly downward-moving — because of the heaviness of earth and the tendency of water to flow downward. Those of mixed nature move in both directions. // Car_1,26.41
[<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s> commentary:]
He states another property of tastes produced by the specific elements with 'Among these' and so on. // 1
'Predominantly' means not all [tastes of that type invariably do so]. // 2
'Tastes' here means substances possessing those tastes. // 3

children.text: plavanatvāditi gatimattvāt yadyapi gatiradho'pi syāt tathāpi laghutvaparigatagatir iha vāyorūrdhvam eva gamanaṃ karoti yathā śālmalītulānām // 4
children.translated_text: 'Floating nature' means having motion. Although motion could also be downward, still, motion accompanied by lightness causes <s>Vāyu</s> to move only upward here — like cotton fibers of the <s>Śālmalī</s> tree. // 4

children.text: hetvantaram āha ūrdhvajvalanatvāc cāgneriti agner apyūrdhvagatitvād ityarthaḥ // 5
children.translated_text: He states another reason with 'and because of the upward-burning nature of fire' — meaning that fire too has an upward tendency. // 5
'Tendency to flow downward' (<s>nimnagavatva</s>) is simply the tendency to move downward. // 6]

children.text: teṣāṃ ṣaṇṇāṃ rasānāmekaikasya yathādravyaṃ guṇakarmāṇyanuvyākhyāsyāmaḥ // Car_1,26.42
children.translated_text: Of those six tastes, we shall explain the qualities and actions of each one, substance by substance. // Car_1,26.42
[<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s> commentary:]

children.text: yathādravyamiti yadyasya rasasya dravyam ādhāras tadanatikrameṇa // 1
children.translated_text: 'Substance by substance' means without transgressing the substance — i.e., the substrate — of each taste. // 1

children.text: etena rasānāṃ guṇakarmaṇī rasādhāre dravye boddhavye iti darśayati // 2]
children.translated_text: By this, [the author] shows that the qualities and actions of tastes should be understood [as belonging to] the substance that is the substrate of the taste. // 2]

children.text: tatra madhuro rasaḥ śarīrasātmyād rasarudhiramāṃsamedo'sthimajjaujaḥśukrābhivardhana āyuṣyaḥ ṣaḍindriyaprasādano balavarṇakaraḥ pittaviṣamārutaghnas tṛṣṇādāhapraśamanas tvacyaḥ keśyaḥ kaṇṭhyo balyaḥ prīṇano jīvanastarpaṇo bṛṃhaṇaḥ sthairyakaraḥ kṣīṇakṣatasaṃdhānakaro ghrāṇamukhakaṇṭhauṣṭhajihvāprahlādano dāhamūrchāpraśamanaḥ ṣaṭpadapipīlikānām iṣṭatamaḥ snigdhaḥ śīto guruśca /
children.translated_text: There, the sweet taste — being congenial to the body — augments plasma (<s>rasa</s>), blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, vitality (<s>ojas</s>), and semen; promotes longevity; pleases the six senses; gives strength and complexion; destroys <s>Pitta</s>, poison, and <s>Vāta</s> (wind); quenches thirst and burning; is beneficial for the skin; good for the hair; good for the throat; strengthening; nourishing; life-giving; satisfying; bulk-promoting; stabilizing; heals the emaciated and wounded; delights the nose, mouth, throat, lips, and tongue; allays burning and fainting; is most beloved of bees and ants; is unctuous, cold, and heavy.
[<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s> commentary:]
'There' and so on. // 1

children.text: madhura ādāv ucyate praśastāyuṣyādiguṇatayā prāyaḥ prāṇipriyatayā ca // 2
children.translated_text: The sweet is stated first because of its praiseworthy qualities such as promoting longevity, and because it is generally most pleasing to living beings. // 2
'Six senses' means including the mind. // 3
'Life-giving' (<s>jīvana</s>) means reviving one who has fainted from injury and the like. // 4
'Promoting longevity' means by being a cause of the extension of lifespan. // 5

children.text: kṣīṇasya saṃdhānakaro dhātupoṣakatvena kiṃvā kṣīṇaścāsau kṣataśceti tena kṣīṇakṣatasya uraḥkṣataṃ saṃdadhāti // 6
children.translated_text: 'Heals the emaciated' — by nourishing the <s>dhātus</s>. Or alternatively, '<s>kṣīṇa</s>' (emaciated) and '<s>kṣata</s>' (wounded) [together mean]: it heals chest-wounds of the emaciated-and-wounded. // 6
The statement of the quality of being desired by bees and the like is useful for knowledge of diseases like <s>prameha</s> (urinary disorders) and the like. // 7

children.text: yaduktaṃ mūtre 'bhidhāvanti pipīlikāśca iti tathā riṣṭe vakṣyati yasmin gṛdhnanti makṣikāḥ iti anena ca madhuratvaṃ jñāyate // 8
children.translated_text: As stated: 'ants rush toward the urine' — and it will be stated in the section on fatal signs: 'that toward which flies are attracted.' By this, sweetness [of urine etc.] is known. // 8

children.text: akṣyāmayenaivābhiṣyande labdhe viśeṣopādānārthaṃ punarvacanaṃ kiṃvā abhiṣyando nāsādiṣvapi jñeyaḥ // 9]
children.translated_text: [The mention of] eye disease in the context of <s>abhiṣyanda</s> (ocular discharge) already obtained — the repetition is for the purpose of specifying a distinction. Or alternatively, <s>abhiṣyanda</s> should be understood [as occurring] in the nose and the like as well. // 9]

children.text: sa evaṃguṇo'pyeka evātyarthamupayujyamānaḥ sthaulyaṃ mārdavam ālasyam atisvapnaṃ gauravamanannābhilāṣam agnerdaurbalyamāsyakaṇṭhayormāṃsābhivṛddhiṃ śvāsakāsapratiśyāyālasakaśītajvarānāhāsyamādhuryavamathusaṃjñāsvarapraṇāśagalagaṇḍagaṇḍamālāślīpadagalaśophabastidhamanīgalopalepākṣyāmayābhiṣyandān ityevaṃprabhṛtīn kaphajān vikārānupajanayati amlo raso bhaktaṃ rocayati agniṃ dīpayati dehaṃ bṛṃhayati ūrjayati mano bodhayati indriyāṇi dṛḍhīkaroti balaṃ vardhayati vātamanulomayati hṛdayaṃ tarpayati āsyamāsrāvayati bhuktamapakarṣayati kledayati jarayati prīṇayati laghuruṣṇaḥ snigdhaśca /
children.translated_text: That [sweet taste], though endowed with such qualities, when used excessively by itself alone, produces: obesity, flabbiness, laziness, excessive sleep, heaviness, loss of appetite, weakness of digestive fire, excessive growth of flesh in the mouth and throat, dyspnea, cough, cold, sluggish bowels, cold-fever, abdominal distension, sweetness of the mouth, nausea, loss of voice, goiter, cervical lymphadenitis, elephantiasis, throat-swelling, urinary-tract disorders, arterial coatings, pharyngeal obstructions, eye-diseases, and <s>abhiṣyanda</s> (discharges) — and similar <s>Kapha</s>-born disorders. The sour taste makes food relishing, kindles the digestive fire, nourishes the body, invigorates, awakens the mind, strengthens the sense-organs, increases strength, normalizes <s>Vāta</s>, satisfies the heart, causes salivation in the mouth, propels the ingested [food] downward, moistens, digests, and gratifies. It is light, hot, and unctuous.
<s>Carakasaṃhitā</s>, <s>Sūtrasthāna</s>, 26 [<s>Ātreyabhadrakāpyīya</s>]
'Satisfies the heart' means it is cordial (<s>hṛdya</s>). // 1

children.text: bhuktam apakarṣayatīti sārayati kledayati tathā jarayati bhuktameva // 2
children.translated_text: 'Propels the ingested [food] downward' means it moves it along; 'moistens' likewise, and 'digests' — [these pertain to] the ingested food itself. // 2

children.text: avamūtritaṃ mūtraviṣairjantubhiḥ parisarpitaṃ ca sparśaviśeṣaiḥ kāraṇḍādibhiḥ // 3]
children.translated_text: '[Urine] contaminated and crawled upon' — [means] crawled upon by creatures [born from] urinary toxins, and by touch-specific [creatures] such as <s>Kāraṇḍa</s> birds and the like. // 3]

children.text: sa evaṃguṇo'pyeka evātyarthamupayujyamāno dantān harṣayati tarṣayati saṃmīlayatyakṣiṇī saṃvejayati lomāni kaphaṃ vilāpayati pittamabhivardhayati raktaṃ dūṣayati māṃsaṃ vidahati kāyaṃ śithilīkaroti kṣīṇakṣatakṛśadurbalānāṃ śvayathum āpādayati api ca kṣatābhihatadaṣṭadagdhabhagnaśūnapracyutāvamūtritaparisarpitamarditacchinnabhinnaviśliṣṭodviddhotpiṣṭādīni pācayatyāgneyasvabhāvāt paridahati kaṇṭhamuro hṛdayaṃ ca lavaṇo rasaḥ pācanaḥ kledano dīpanaścyāvanaśchedano bhedanas tīkṣṇaḥ saro vikāsy adhaḥsraṃsy avakāśakaro vātaharaḥ stambhabandhasaṃghātavidhamanaḥ sarvarasapratyanīkabhūtaḥ āsyamāsrāvayati kaphaṃ viṣyandayati mārgān viśodhayati sarvaśarīrāvayavān mṛdūkaroti rocayatyāhāram āhārayogī nātyarthaṃ guruḥ snigdha uṣṇaśca /
children.translated_text: Though possessing such qualities, the salty taste alone, when used excessively, causes tingling in the teeth, produces thirst, makes the eyes close, causes horripilation, liquefies <s>kapha</s> (phlegm), increases <s>pitta</s> (bile), vitiates the blood, burns the flesh, loosens the body, and produces swelling in the emaciated, wounded, thin, and weak. Moreover, it causes suppuration in wounds, those struck, bitten, burned, fractured, swollen, dislocated, those with urinary disorders, those with spreading skin diseases, those bruised, cut, split, disjointed, pierced, and crushed — and because of its fiery nature, it burns the throat, chest, and heart. The salty taste is digestive, moistening, appetizing, secreting, penetrating, splitting, sharp, flowing, expanding, downward-moving, space-creating, <s>vāta</s>-destroying, and dispersive of stiffness, binding, and solidification. It is the antithesis of all other tastes. It causes salivation in the mouth, liquefies <s>kapha</s>, clears the channels, softens all body-parts, stimulates appetite — it is always suitable for food. It is not excessively heavy; it is unctuous and hot.
[<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s> commentary:]
'Expanding' (<s>vikāsī</s>) means: causing dissolution by moisture. // 1
'Downward-moving' (<s>adhaḥsraṃsī</s>) means: having the nature of liquefying [downward]. // 2

children.text: sarvarasapratyanīkabhūta iti yatra mātrātirikto lavaṇo bhavati tatra nānyo rasa upalakṣyate // 3
children.translated_text: 'The antithesis of all other tastes' — where the salty taste exceeds the proper measure, there no other taste is perceived. // 3
'Suitable for food' (<s>āhārayogī</s>) means: it is always combined with food. // 4
'Confuses' (<s>mohayati</s>) means: causes disturbance. // 5
'Causes fainting' (<s>mūrchayati</s>) means: causes loss of consciousness. // 6]

children.text: sa evaṃguṇo'pyeka evātyartham upayujyamānaḥ pittaṃ kopayati raktaṃ vardhayati tarṣayati mūrchayati tāpayati dārayati kuṣṇāti māṃsāni pragālayati kuṣṭhāni viṣaṃ vardhayati śophān sphoṭayati dantāṃścyāvayati puṃstvamupahanti indriyāṇyuparuṇaddhi valipalitakhālityamāpādayati api ca lohitapittāmlapittavīsarpavātaraktavicarcikendraluptaprabhṛtīn vikārān upajanayati kaṭuko raso vaktraṃ śodhayati agniṃ dīpayati bhuktaṃ śoṣayati ghrāṇamāsrāvayati cakṣurvirecayati sphuṭīkarotīndriyāṇi alasakaśvayathūpacayodardābhiṣyandasnehasvedakledamalān upahanti rocayatyaśanaṃ kaṇḍūrvināśayati vraṇān avasādayati krimīn hinasti māṃsaṃ vilikhati śoṇitasaṃghātaṃ bhinatti bandhāṃśchinatti mārgān vivṛṇoti śleṣmāṇaṃ śamayati laghuruṣṇo rūkṣaśca /
children.translated_text: Though possessing such qualities, the pungent taste alone, when used excessively, aggravates <s>pitta</s>, increases blood, produces thirst, causes fainting, heats, tears [the tissues], shrivels, dissolves the flesh, liquefies [tissues], promotes skin diseases, increases poison, bursts open swellings, loosens teeth, destroys virility, obstructs the sense-organs, and produces wrinkles, grey hair, and baldness. Moreover, it generates disorders such as <s>lohitapitta</s> (hemorrhagic disease), <s>amlapitta</s> (acid reflux), <s>vīsarpa</s> (erysipelas), <s>vātarakta</s> (gout), <s>vicarcikā</s> (eczema), <s>indralupta</s> (alopecia), and the like. The pungent taste cleanses the mouth, kindles the digestive fire, dries what is eaten, causes nasal secretion, purges the eyes, sharpens the sense-organs, destroys <s>alasaka</s> (torpor), swelling, accumulation, urticaria, excessive moisture, unctuousness, sweat, moisture, and impurities. It stimulates appetite, destroys itching, reduces wounds, kills worms, scrapes away flesh, breaks up blood-clots, cuts bonds, opens the channels, pacifies <s>śleṣman</s> (phlegm). It is light, hot, and dry.

children.text: sa evaṃguṇo'pyeka evātyarthamupayujyamāno vipākaprabhāvāt puṃstvamupahanti rasavīryaprabhāvānmohayanti glāpayati sādayati karśayati mūrchayati namayati tamayati bhramayati kaṇṭhaṃ paridahati śarīratāpamupajanayati balaṃ kṣiṇoti tṛṣṇāṃ janayati api ca vāyvagniguṇabāhulyād bhramadavathukampatodabhedaiś caraṇabhujapārśvapṛṣṭhaprabhṛtiṣu mārutajān vikārān upajanayati tikto rasaḥ svayamarociṣṇur apyarocakaghno viṣaghnaḥ krimighno mūrchādāhakaṇḍūkuṣṭhatṛṣṇāpraśamanas tvaṅmāṃsayoḥ sthirīkaraṇo jvaraghno dīpanaḥ pācanaḥ stanyaśodhano lekhanaḥ kledamedovasāmajjalasīkāpūyasvedamūtrapurīṣapittaśleṣmopaśoṣaṇo rūkṣaḥ śīto laghuśca /
children.translated_text: Though possessing such qualities, the bitter taste alone, when used excessively — by the power of its <s>vipāka</s> (post-digestive effect) destroys virility; by the power of its taste and potency, it confuses, enfeebles, exhausts, emacitates, causes fainting, bending, darkness, dizziness, burns the throat, generates bodily heat, depletes strength, and produces thirst. Moreover, because of the predominance of <s>vāyu</s> (wind) and <s>agni</s> (fire) qualities, it generates <s>vāta</s>-born disorders in the feet, arms, sides, back, and the like — through dizziness, burning, trembling, pricking pain, and splitting. The bitter taste, though itself unpalatable, is a destroyer of loss of appetite; it destroys poison, destroys worms, pacifies fainting, burning, itching, skin diseases, and thirst; it makes the skin and flesh firm; it destroys fever; it is appetizing and digestive; it purifies breast-milk; it is scraping; it dries up moisture, fat, marrow, lymph, pus, sweat, urine, feces, <s>pitta</s>, and <s>kapha</s>. It is dry, cold, and light.

children.text: sa evaṃguṇo'pyeka evātyarthamupayujyamāno raukṣyāt kharaviṣadasvabhāvāc ca rasarudhiramāṃsamedo'sthimajjaśukrāṇy ucchoṣayati srotasāṃ kharatvamupapādayati balam ādatte karśayati glapayati mohayati bhramayati vadanam upaśoṣayati aparāṃśca vātavikārānupajanayati kaṣāyo rasaḥ saṃśamanaḥ saṃgrāhī saṃdhānakaraḥ pīḍano ropaṇaḥ śoṣaṇaḥ stambhanaḥ śleṣmaraktapittapraśamanaḥ śarīrakledasyopayoktā rūkṣaḥ śīto'laghuśca /
children.translated_text: Though possessing such qualities, the astringent taste alone, when used excessively — because of its dryness and rough, clear nature — desiccates <s>rasa</s> (plasma), blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen; produces roughness in the channels; takes away strength; causes emaciation, enfeeblement, confusion, and dizziness; dries up the mouth; and generates other <s>vāta</s> disorders as well. The astringent taste is pacifying, absorbing, healing, pressing, wound-healing, drying, styptic; it pacifies <s>kapha</s>, blood, and <s>pitta</s>; it utilizes bodily moisture. It is dry, cold, and not light.

children.text: sa evaṃguṇo'pyeka evātyarthamupayujyamāna āsyaṃ śoṣayati hṛdayaṃ pīḍayati udaram ādhmāpayati vācaṃ nigṛhṇāti srotāṃsy avabadhnāti śyāvatvamāpādayati puṃstvamupahanti viṣṭabhya jarāṃ gacchati vātamūtrapurīṣaretāṃsyavagṛhṇāti karśayati glapayati tarṣayati stambhayati kharaviśadarūkṣatvāt pakṣavadhagrahāpatānakārditaprabhṛtīṃś ca vātavikārānupajanayati // 43
children.translated_text: Though possessing such qualities, the astringent taste alone, when used excessively, dries the mouth, presses the heart, causes abdominal distension, suppresses speech, obstructs the channels, produces dark discoloration, destroys virility, retards digestion, obstructs wind, urine, feces, and semen, causes emaciation, enfeeblement, thirst, and rigidity — and because of its rough, clear, and dry nature, generates <s>vāta</s> disorders such as hemiplegia, spasms, convulsions, facial paralysis, and the like. // 43
[{<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s>}

children.text: vipākasya prabhāvo vipākaprabhāvaḥ vipākaśca kaṭūnāṃ kaṭureva rasasya vīryasya ca prabhāvo rasavīryaprabhāvaḥ ayaṃ ca vakṣyamāṇe sarvatra hetuḥ // 1
children.translated_text: The power of <s>vipāka</s> is the <s>vipāka-prabhāva</s> (effect of post-digestive transformation). And the <s>vipāka</s> of pungent [tastes] is indeed pungent itself. The power of taste and potency is the <s>rasa-vīrya-prabhāva</s>. This is the cause in all [cases] to be mentioned hereafter. // 1
The direct mention of the feet and the like is because <s>vāta</s> disorders predominantly [occur] there. // 2

children.text: atra ca vipākaprabhāvādikathanam udāharaṇārthaṃ tena madhurādiṣu vipākādikāryam unneyam // 3
children.translated_text: And here, the mention of the effects of <s>vipāka</s> and the like is for the purpose of illustration. From this, the effects of <s>vipāka</s> and the like in sweet tastes etc. should be inferred. // 3
'Enfeebles' (<s>glapayati</s>) means: causes loss of enthusiasm. // 4
'Pressing' (<s>pīḍana</s>) means: pressing upon wounds. // 5
'Utilizes bodily moisture' (<s>śarīrakledasyopayoktā</s>) means: absorbs [it]. // 6
'Cold and not light' (<s>śīto'laghuśca</s>) — by the coalescence of the vowel <s>a</s>, [it reads] 'not light' (<s>alaghu</s>). // 7
'Obstructs' (<s>avagṛhṇāti</s>) means: makes [them] bound. // 8]

children.text: ityevamete ṣaḍrasāḥ pṛthaktvenaikatvena vā mātraśaḥ samyagupayujyamānā upakārāya bhavantyadhyātmalokasya apakārakarāḥ punarato'nyathā bhavantyupayujyamānāḥ tān vidvānupakārārthameva mātraśaḥ samyagupayojayediti // Car_1,26.44
children.translated_text: Thus these six tastes, used properly in [correct] measure — whether separately or combined — are beneficial to the body-self-world. But used otherwise [i.e., improperly], they become harmful. The wise man should therefore employ them in proper measure, for the purpose of benefit alone. // Car_1,26.44
[{<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s>}
'Separately' (<s>pṛthaktvena</s>) means: one by one, in measure. // 1
'Combined' (<s>ekatvena</s>) means: combined together — in the measure of the aggregate — such is the meaning. // 2
'In measure' (<s>mātraśaḥ</s>) means: with [proper] dosage. // 3
And that combination should be understood as with two, three, or all [tastes]. // 4
'Of the body-self-world' (<s>adhyātmalokasya</s>) means: of all living beings. // 5
'Otherwise' (<s>anyathā</s>) means: without [proper] measure. // 6]

children.text: śītaṃ vīryeṇa yad dravyaṃ madhuraṃ rasapākayoḥ /
children.translated_text: That substance which is cold in potency and sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect;

children.text: tayoramlaṃ yaduṣṇaṃ ca yaddravyaṃ kaṭukaṃ tayoḥ // Car_1,26.45
children.translated_text: that which is sour in both [taste and vipāka] and hot; and that substance which is pungent in both — // Car_1,26.45
[{<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s>}

children.text: samprati rasadvāreṇaiva dravyāṇāṃ vīryam āha śītamityādi // 1
children.translated_text: Now, through the medium of taste itself, he states the potency of substances, with 'cold' and the rest. // 1

children.text: yaddravyaṃ rase pāke ca madhuraṃ tacchītaṃ vīryeṇa jñeyaṃ tathā tayoriti rasapākayor yadamlaṃ dravyaṃ taduṣṇaṃ vīryeṇa tathā yacca dravyaṃ tayoriti rasapākayoḥ kaṭukam uktaṃ taccoṣṇaṃ vīryeṇa bhavati iti śeṣaḥ // 2
children.translated_text: That substance which is sweet in taste and in <s>vipāka</s> (post-digestive effect) should be known as cold in potency. Likewise, 'in both' means in taste and <s>vipāka</s> — that substance which is sour is hot in potency. And that substance which is pungent 'in both' — in taste and <s>vipāka</s> — is also hot in potency: this is the remainder [of the sentence]. // 2

children.text: kiṃvā yaccoṣṇaṃ kaṭukaṃ tayoḥ iti pāṭhaḥ // 3
children.translated_text: Or the reading is: 'that which is hot and pungent in both.' // 3

children.text: tatra yadrasato madhuraṃ tad vīryataḥ śītamiti vaktavye yad rasapākayor iti karoti tan madhurarasocitapākasyaiva madhuradravyasya śītavīryatāprāptyartham evam amlakaṭukayor api vācyam // 4]
children.translated_text: There, whereas it should be said 'what is sweet in taste is cold in potency,' he says 'in taste and <s>vipāka</s>' — this is for the purpose of establishing that only a sweet substance whose <s>vipāka</s> is also appropriate to sweetness [i.e., also sweet] has cold potency. The same should be said for sour and pungent. // 4]
The collection of properties of those [substances] should be indicated by instruction about taste —
of those that are not contrary in potency and in <s>vipāka</s> [to their taste], this will be taught. // Car_1,26.46

children.text: yathā payo yathā sarpir yathā vā cavyacitrakau /
children.translated_text: Just as milk, just as ghee, just as <s>cavya</s> and <s>citraka</s> (long pepper and leadwort) —
such and other [substances] the physician should indicate by taste. // Car_1,26.47
[{<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s>}

children.text: teṣām iti madhurapākādīnāṃ rasopadeśeneti rasamātrakathanenaiva yato vipāko 'pi rasata eva prāyo jñāyate yad vakṣyati kaṭutiktakaṣāyāṇāṃ vipākaḥ prāyaśaḥ kaṭur ityādi // 1
children.translated_text: 'Of those' means: of sweet-in-<s>vipāka</s> etc. 'By instruction about taste' means: by the statement of taste alone. Since <s>vipāka</s> too is generally known through taste — for it will be stated: 'The <s>vipāka</s> of pungent, bitter, and astringent is generally pungent' and so on. // 1
But this is not [applicable] in all cases — this he states with 'in potency' and the rest. // 2

children.text: vīryato'viparītānāṃ rasadvārā vīryajñānaṃ na tu rasaviruddhavīryāṇāṃ mahāpañcamūlādīnāṃ na kevalaṃ rasena kiṃ tarhi pākataśca ya upadekṣyate guṇasaṃgrahaḥ śukrahā baddhaviṇmūtro vipāko vātalaḥ kaṭuḥ ityādinā sa ca vīryato 'viruddhānāṃ vijñeyaḥ yadi tatra vīryaṃ virodhi bhavati tadā vipāko'pi yathoktaguṇakarī na syāt // 3
children.translated_text: 'Of those not contrary in potency' — knowledge of potency through taste [applies only to] those whose potency is not contrary to their taste, not to those like <s>mahāpañcamūla</s> whose potency contradicts their taste. Not by taste alone — but 'also by <s>vipāka</s>' the collection of properties which will be taught [is known]: '<s>Vipāka</s> that is pungent destroys semen, binds feces and urine, and aggravates <s>vāta</s>' and so on. And that [knowledge through <s>vipāka</s>] too should be understood [only] for those not contrary in potency. If potency is contradictory, then <s>vipāka</s> too would not produce the stated qualities. // 3

children.text: kiṃvā pākataścāviparītānāṃ rasopadeśena guṇasaṃgrahaḥ śītoṣṇalakṣaṇo nirdeśyaḥ yasyāstu pippalyāḥ kaṭukāyā api viparītamadhurapākitvaṃ na tatra kaṭu rasatvenoṣṇatvam ityarthaḥ // 4
children.translated_text: Or: 'Of those not contrary [also] in <s>vipāka</s> — the collection of properties, characterized as cold or hot, should be indicated by instruction about taste.' But for <s>pippalī</s> (long pepper), which though pungent in taste has a contrary sweet <s>vipāka</s> — its pungent taste does not [necessarily mean] hotness: such is the meaning. // 4

children.text: asmiṃśca pakṣe upadekṣyate iti yathā payaḥ ityādinā sambadhyate // 5
children.translated_text: And in this interpretation, 'will be taught' is connected with 'just as milk' and so on. // 5
He states those very [substances] having non-contrary potency and <s>vipāka</s> with 'just as milk' and so on. // 6
For milk and the like, in the context of stating substance-properties, are to be taught as having non-contrary potency and <s>vipāka</s>. // 7]
[{<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s>}

children.text: samprati madhuratiktakaṣāyāṇāṃ śītatvaṃ tathā kaṭvamlalavaṇānāṃ coṣṇatvaṃ tathā kaṭutiktakaṣāyāṇāṃ cāvṛṣyatvamityādayo rasadvāreṇa dravyāṇāṃ ye guṇā uktāstadapavādam āha teṣāmityādi // 1
children.translated_text: Now, the coldness of sweet, bitter, and astringent [tastes], as well as the hotness of pungent, sour, and salty [tastes], and the non-aphrodisiac nature of pungent, bitter, and astringent — these properties of substances stated through the medium of taste — he states an exception to these with 'of those' and the rest. // 1

children.text: rasopadeśena rasaguṇakathanadvāreṇa dravyāṇāṃ yaḥ śītoṣṇādiguṇasaṃgrahaḥ kṛtaḥ sa vīryataḥ pākataścāviparītānāṃ teṣāṃ vakṣyamāṇakṣīrādidravyāṇāmeva nirdeṣṭuṃ śakyaḥ na tu rasaviparītavīryavipākānām ityarthaḥ // 2
children.translated_text: 'By instruction about taste' — through the medium of stating taste-properties — the collection of cold, hot, and other qualities of substances that has been made — that can be indicated [by taste alone] only for those [substances] that are 'not contrary in potency and in <s>vipāka</s>' — namely the forthcoming milk and other substances — not for those whose potency and <s>vipāka</s> are contrary to their taste: such is the meaning. // 2
He instructs [about] those having non-contrary potency and <s>vipāka</s> with 'will be taught' and the rest. // 3

children.text: upadekṣyata iti yathā paya ityādibhiḥ sambadhyate // 4
children.translated_text: 'Will be taught' is connected with 'just as milk' and so on. // 4

children.text: etāni hi dravyaguṇakathanaprasaṅge rasāviparītavīryavipākatayaivopadeṣṭavyānīti rasānurūpaguṇatvam eṣāṃ jñātavyam ityarthaḥ // 5
children.translated_text: For these, in the context of stating substance-properties, are to be taught only as having potency and <s>vipāka</s> not contrary to their taste — hence the taste-concordant nature of their properties should be known: such is the meaning. // 5

children.text: idaṃ tūdāharaṇaikadeśamātraṃ tenāparāṇy apyevaṃjātīyāny udāhartavyānītyāha evamādīnītyādi // 6
children.translated_text: But this is merely a partial illustration; therefore other substances of this kind too are to be illustrated — this he states with 'such and other' and the rest. // 6
'Such and other' means: of such a kind — wheat and the like: such is the meaning. // 7]

children.text: madhuraṃ kiṃciduṣṇaṃ syāt kaṣāyaṃ tiktameva ca /
children.translated_text: Some sweet [substances] are hot; and astringent and bitter too [may be hot] —
for example, <s>mahāpañcamūla</s> (the five great roots), and also lotus-lake and marshy meats. // Car_1,26.48
The salty <s>saindhava</s> (rock-salt) is not hot; and sour <s>āmalaka</s> (Indian gooseberry) likewise;
among bitter ones — <s>arka</s>, <s>aguru</s>, and <s>guḍūcī</s> — their bitterness is declared to be hot. // Car_1,26.49
[{<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s>}

children.text: samprati yatra viruddhavīryatvena rasenoṣṇatvādi na nirdeśyaṃ tad āha madhuram ityādi // 1
children.translated_text: Now, where hotness etc. cannot be indicated by taste because of having contrary potency — he states that with 'sweet' and the rest. // 1

children.text: kiṃcit kaṣāyaṃ coṣṇaṃ tiktaṃ coṣṇam iti yojanā kaṣāyatiktalavaṇānām udāharaṇam asūtritānām api prakaraṇāt kṛtam // 2
children.translated_text: 'Some astringent also is hot, and bitter also is hot' — this is the syntactic connection. The examples for astringent, bitter, and salty [being hot] — though not stated in sūtra form — are given from the context. // 2
'<s>Mahāpañcamūla</s>' means the <s>pañcamūla</s> beginning with <s>bilva</s> (Aegle marmelos) here. // 3

children.text: etacca tiktasya kaṣāyasya coṣṇatāyām udāharaṇam abjānūpāmiṣaṃ tu madhurasyoṣṇavīryatve // 4]
children.translated_text: And this is an example of the hotness of bitter and astringent [tastes]; but lotus-lake and marshy meats are [an example] of sweet [taste] having hot potency. // 4]

children.text: kiṃcidamlaṃ hi saṃgrāhi kiṃcidamlaṃ bhinatti ca /
children.translated_text: Some sour [substances] are astringent [in action]; some sour ones are purgative —

children.text: yathā kapitthaṃ saṃgrāhi bhedi cāmalakaṃ tathā // Car_1,26.50
children.translated_text: just as <s>kapittha</s> (wood-apple) is astringent, and <s>āmalaka</s> (Indian gooseberry) is purgative. // Car_1,26.50
<s>Pippalī</s> (long pepper) and <s>nāgara</s> (dry ginger) are aphrodisiac, though pungent [taste] is said to be non-aphrodisiac;

children.text: kaṣāyaḥ stambhanaḥ śītaḥ so 'bhayāyām ato'nyathā // Car_1,26.51
children.translated_text: astringent [taste] is styptic and cold — but in <s>abhayā</s> (<s>harītakī</s>), it is otherwise. // Car_1,26.51
Therefore, one should not prescribe every substance [merely] by instruction about taste;

children.text: dṛṣṭaṃ tulyarase'pyevaṃ dravye dravye guṇāntaram // Car_1,26.52
children.translated_text: for even in substances of the same taste, diversity of properties is observed in each substance. // Car_1,26.52
[{<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s>}

children.text: vīryaprasaṅgād anyam apyamlādīnāṃ viruddhaguṇam āha kiṃcid ityādi // 1
children.translated_text: In the context of potency, he states another contradictory quality of sour and other [tastes] with 'some' and the rest. // 1

children.text: abhayāyām ato'nyatheti abhayāyāṃ kaṣāyo raso bhedanaś coṣṇaś cetyarthaḥ // 2]
children.translated_text: 'In <s>abhayā</s>, it is otherwise' means: in <s>abhayā</s> (<s>harītakī</s>), the astringent taste is purgative and hot: such is the meaning. // 2]
Because of dryness, the astringent is supreme among dry [tastes]; pungent is middling;
bitter is the least. Among hot [tastes], because of heat, salty is the foremost. // Car_1,26.53

children.text: madhyo'mlaḥ kaṭukaś cāntyaḥ snigdhānāṃ madhuraḥ paraḥ /
children.translated_text: Sour is middling; pungent is the last. Among unctuous [tastes], sweet is foremost;
sour is middling; and salty is the last taste — declared [thus] because of unctuousness. // Car_1,26.54
Among cold [tastes], middling, foremost, and least — because of coldness — are astringent, sweet, and bitter respectively.
Due to heaviness, sweet exceeds astringent; salt is the lowest [among the heavy]. // Car_1,26.55
Pungent is [lighter] than sour, and then bitter — due to lightness — is the best of the best;

children.text: kecil laghūnām avaramicchanti lavaṇaṃ rasam // Car_1,26.56
children.translated_text: some consider salt to be the lowest among the light [rasas]. // Car_1,26.56
But in both heaviness and lightness, it [salt] is the lowest of both.
[<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s> commentary:
'Due to dryness,' etc. // 1

children.text: raukṣyeṇa kaṣāya uttama iti rūkṣatamaḥ tikto rūkṣaḥ kaṭustu madhyo rūkṣataraḥ evam anyatrāpi // 2
children.translated_text: By dryness, astringent is the highest, i.e., the driest; bitter is dry; but pungent is intermediate, i.e., drier [than sweet but less than astringent]. Similarly in other [categories] as well. // 2
'And pungent is the last' means the lowest — this is the meaning. // 3
'And salt is the last' means the lowest — this is the meaning. // 4
'Salt is the lowest' means by heaviness — this is the meaning. // 5

children.text: amlāt kaṭur ityādau amlātkaṭurlaghuḥ tataḥ kaṭukād uttamāt tikto laghutvenottamottamaḥ uttamāt kaṭukāduttama uttamottamaḥ // 6
children.translated_text: In 'pungent is [lighter] than sour' etc.: pungent is lighter than sour; then bitter, [lighter] than pungent which is the best, is, due to lightness, the best of the best — better than pungent, which is already the best. // 6
He states an alternative view with 'some,' etc. // 7
He accepts that alternative view by the turn of phrase, saying 'in heaviness,' etc. // 8

children.text: etena gaurave lāghave cāvaratvaṃ lavaṇasya svīkurvan gaurave 'vara ityanenāmlakaṭutiktebhyo gurutvaṃ svīkaroti lavaṇasya lāghave cāvara ityanenāmlādapi laghuno 'lpaṃ lāghavaṃ lavaṇasya svīkaroti // 9
children.translated_text: By this, accepting that salt is the lowest in both heaviness and lightness: 'lowest in heaviness' — by this he accepts that salt is heavier than sour, pungent, and bitter; 'and lowest in lightness' — by this he accepts that salt has slightly less lightness than even sour, which is light. // 9

children.text: na ca vācyam amle pṛthivī kāraṇaṃ lavaṇe tu toyaṃ tataḥ pṛthivyapekṣayā toyajanyasya lavaṇasyaiva lāghavamucitamiti yato na niveśena gauravalāghave śakyete 'vadhārayituṃ tathāhi toyātirekakṛto madhuraḥ pṛthivyatirekakṛtāt kaṣāyādgururbhavati // 10]
children.translated_text: And one should not object: 'In sour, earth is the cause; in salt, water. Therefore, lightness would be more fitting for salt, which is water-born, compared to earth.' For heaviness and lightness cannot be determined by the [elemental] composition [alone]; for instance, sweet, which is made with a preponderance of water, is heavier than astringent, which is made with a preponderance of earth. // 10]

children.text: paraṃ cāto vipākānāṃ lakṣaṇaṃ sampravakṣyate // Car_1,26.57
children.translated_text: And hereafter, the characteristics of <s>vipākas</s> (post-digestive effects) will be described. // Car_1,26.57
The <s>vipāka</s> of pungent, bitter, and astringent is generally pungent;
sour is digested as sour; sweet [is digested as] sweet, and salty likewise. // Car_1,26.58
[<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s> commentary:
Now, since <s>vipāka</s> too has the nature of <s>rasa</s>, he states its characteristics beginning with 'and hereafter,' etc. // 1

By the use of the word 'generally' (<s>prāya</s>), he indicates that [substances like] long pepper (<s>pippalī</s>), horse gram (<s>kulattha</s>), etc. have a <s>vipāka</s> that does not follow their <s>rasa</s>. // 2

children.text: kaṭukādiśabdena ca tadādhāraṃ dravyamucyate yato na rasāḥ pacyante kiṃtu dravyam eva // 3
children.translated_text: By the term 'pungent, etc.,' it is the substance that is their substrate that is meant, because it is not the <s>rasas</s> that are digested, but the substance itself. // 3
'Salty likewise' means salt too generally has a sweet <s>vipāka</s> — this is the meaning. // 4

children.text: vipākalakṣaṇaṃ tu jaṭharāgniyogād āhārasya niṣṭhākāle yo guṇa utpadyate sa vipākaḥ vacanaṃ hi /
children.translated_text: The definition of <s>vipāka</s> is: the quality that arises at the final stage of digestion of food through the action of the digestive fire (<s>jaṭharāgni</s>) — that is <s>vipāka</s>. For the statement says:
'That different taste which arises through the action of the gastric fire
at the end of the transformation of food — that is declared to be <s>vipāka</s>.' // 5]

children.text: madhuro lavaṇāmlau ca snigdhabhāvāt trayo rasāḥ /
children.translated_text: Sweet, salty, and sour — three <s>rasas</s>, due to their unctuous nature,

children.text: vātamūtrapurīṣāṇāṃ prāyo mokṣe sukhā matāḥ // Car_1,26.59
children.translated_text: are generally considered to facilitate the comfortable passage of <s>vāta</s> (flatus), urine, and feces. // Car_1,26.59
But pungent, bitter, and astringent — three <s>rasas</s>, due to their dry nature,
are seen to cause difficulty in the passage of <s>vāta</s>, feces, urine, and semen. // Car_1,26.60
[<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s> commentary:

children.text: samprati vakṣyamāṇavipākalakṣaṇe madhurāmlapākayor vātamūtrapurīṣān avarodhakatve tathā kaṭorvipākasya vātamūtrapurīṣavibandhakatve hetum āha madhura ityādi // 1
children.translated_text: Now, he states the reason for the properties described regarding the <s>vipāka</s> characteristics to be stated — viz., that sweet and sour <s>vipākas</s> do not obstruct <s>vāta</s>, urine, and feces, while pungent <s>vipāka</s> causes obstruction of <s>vāta</s>, urine, and feces — beginning with 'sweet,' etc. // 1

children.text: atra madhurāmlalavaṇā niṣṭhāpākaṃ gatā api santaḥ snehaguṇayogād vātapurīṣāṇāṃ visargaṃ sukhena kurvantīti vākyārthaḥ // 2
children.translated_text: Here the sentence means: sweet, sour, and salty, even when they have reached the final stage of digestion, by virtue of their unctuous quality, facilitate the easy passage of <s>vāta</s> and feces. // 2
Therefore, this is the common characteristic of sweet and sour <s>vipāka</s>. // 3
Similarly, in the opposite case — for pungent, bitter, and astringent too — the sentence meaning [is to be understood]. // 4]
Pungent <s>vipāka</s> destroys semen, obstructs feces and urine, and aggravates <s>Vāta</s>;
sweet <s>vipāka</s> facilitates feces and urine, and increases <s>Kapha</s> and semen. // Car_1,26.61
Sour <s>vipāka</s> produces <s>Pitta</s>, facilitates feces and urine, and destroys semen;

children.text: teṣāṃ guruḥ syānmadhuraḥ kaṭukāmlāv ato 'nyathā // Car_1,26.62
children.translated_text: among them, the sweet [<s>vipāka</s>] is heavy; the pungent and sour are otherwise [i.e., light]. // Car_1,26.62
[<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s> commentary:

children.text: samprati vipākalakṣaṇaṃ hetuvyutpāditaṃ śukrahatvādiviśeṣayuktaṃ vaktum āha śukrahetyādi // 1
children.translated_text: Now, to state the <s>vipāka</s> characteristics derived from [their] causes, together with specific properties such as semen-destroying nature, etc., he says 'semen-destroying,' etc. // 1
'Otherwise' means light. // 2]
With respect to the lesser, middling, and abundant [degree] of the <s>vipāka</s> characteristics,
one should observe [them] in each substance, due to the particular distinction of qualities. // Car_1,26.63
[<s>Āyurvedadīpikā</s> commentary:

children.text: samprati yathoktavipākalakṣaṇānāṃ dravyabhede kvacidalpatvaṃ kvacinmadhyatvaṃ kvacic cotkṛṣṭatvaṃ yathā bhavati tad āha vipāketyādi // 1
children.translated_text: Now, how the aforementioned <s>vipāka</s> characteristics may be lesser in some substances, middling in some, and superior in some — that he states with '<s>vipāka</s>,' etc. // 1

children.text: vipākalakṣaṇasyālpamadhyabhūyiṣṭhatām upalakṣayet prati prati dravyāṇāṃ guṇavaiśeṣyāddhetor ityarthaḥ // 2
children.translated_text: One should observe the lesser, middling, and abundant degree of the <s>vipāka</s> characteristics in each substance, due to the cause that is the particular distinction of qualities — this is the meaning. // 2

children.text: etena dravyeṣu yad guṇavaiśeṣyaṃ madhuratvamadhurataratvamadhuratamatvādi tato hetor vipākānāmalpatvādayo viśeṣā bhavantītyuktaṃ bhavati // 3
children.translated_text: By this, it is stated that from the cause which is the particular distinction of qualities in substances — such as sweet, sweeter, sweetest, etc. — the distinctions of lesser degree, etc., of <s>vipākas</s> arise. // 3

children.text: atra kecidbruvate pratirasaṃ pāko bhavati yathā madhurādīnāṃ ṣaṇṇāṃ ṣaṇmadhurādayaḥ pākā iti kecid bruvate balavatāṃ rasānāmabalavanto rasā vaśatāṃ yānti tataś cānavasthitaḥ pākaḥ // 4
children.translated_text: Here, some say that <s>vipāka</s> occurs for each <s>rasa</s> — that is, there are six <s>vipākas</s> — sweet, etc. — for the six [<s>rasas</s>] sweet, etc. Some say that the weaker <s>rasas</s> come under the power of the stronger <s>rasas</s>, and therefore <s>vipāka</s> is unstable. // 4

children.text: tatraitaddvitayamapi pāke vyavasthākaraṇam anādṛtya suśrutena dvividhaḥ pāko madhuraḥ kaṭuś cāṅgīkṛtaḥ // 5
children.translated_text: In this regard, disregarding both of these alternatives for establishing [the number of] <s>vipākas</s>, <s>Suśruta</s> has accepted a twofold <s>vipāka</s>: sweet and pungent. // 5

children.text: dvaividhyaṃ ca pañcabhūtātmake dravye gurubhūtapṛthivītoyātirekānmadhuraḥ pāko bhavati śeṣalaghubhūtātirekāt tu kaṭukaḥ pāko bhavati yaduktaṃ dravyeṣu pacyamāneṣu yeṣv ambupṛthivīguṇāḥ // 6
children.translated_text: And the twofold nature is thus: in a substance composed of the five elements, due to the preponderance of the heavier elements earth and water, the sweet <s>vipāka</s> occurs; and due to the preponderance of the remaining lighter elements, the pungent <s>vipāka</s> occurs. As stated: 'In substances being digested, in which the qualities of water and earth // 6
are produced in excess — there the <s>vipāka</s> is said to be sweet.' // 7
'In those being digested, in which the qualities of fire, wind, and space // 8
are produced in excess — there the <s>vipāka</s> is said to be pungent.' // 9

children.text: pratirasapāke tathānavasthitapāke ca dravyaṃ rasaguṇenaiva tulyaṃ pākāvasthāyāmapi bhavati tena na kaścidviśeṣo vipākena tatra bodhyata iti suśrutena tatpakṣadvayam upekṣitamiti sādhu kṛtam // 10
children.translated_text: In the view of <s>vipāka</s> for each <s>rasa</s>, as well as in the view of unstable <s>vipāka</s>, the substance in the state of <s>vipāka</s> too becomes equivalent to the <s>rasa</s> quality alone; therefore no special [knowledge] is gained from <s>vipāka</s> in that case — thus <s>Suśruta</s> has correctly disregarded both those positions. // 10

children.text: tṛtīyāmlapākanirāsastu doṣam āvahati yato vrīhikulatthādīnām amlapākatayā pittakartṛtvamupalabhyate atha manyase vrīhyāder uṣṇavīryatvena tatra pittakartṛtvaṃ tanna madhurasya vrīhestanmate madhuravipākasyoṣṇavīryatāyāmapi satyāṃ na pittakartṛtvamupapadyate rasavipākābhyām ekasya vīryasya bādhanīyatvāt // 11
children.translated_text: But the rejection of the third — sour <s>vipāka</s> — brings a difficulty, because the <s>Pitta</s>-producing nature of rice (<s>vrīhi</s>), horse gram (<s>kulattha</s>), etc. is observed due to their sour <s>vipāka</s>. If you think that for rice etc., the <s>Pitta</s>-producing nature is due to their hot potency (<s>uṣṇavīrya</s>), that is not so, because in [<s>Suśruta</s>'s] view, rice is sweet, and even with sweet <s>vipāka</s>, if the potency is hot, <s>Pitta</s>-production is not justified, since the potency would be overridden by <s>rasa</s> and <s>vipāka</s> taken together. // 11

children.text: kiṃca amlapākatvād vrīhyādeḥ pittamamlaguṇamutpadyate yadi tu tad uṣṇavīryatākṛtaṃ syāttadā kaṭuguṇabhūyiṣṭhaṃ pittaṃ syāt dṛśyate ca vrīhibhakṣaṇād amlodgārādināmlaguṇabhūyiṣṭhataiveti // 12
children.translated_text: Moreover, if from the sour <s>vipāka</s> of rice etc., <s>Pitta</s> with sour qualities is produced — and if that were caused by hot potency, then the <s>Pitta</s> would have predominantly pungent qualities. But it is observed that from eating rice, sour eructation etc. [result], showing a predominance of sour qualities. // 12

children.text: kiṃca pṛthivīsomaguṇātirekān madhuraḥ pāko bhavati vāyvagnyākāśātirekācca kaṭur bhavatīti pakṣe yadā vyāmiśraguṇātirekatā bhavati tadā somāgnyātmakasyāmlasyotpādaḥ kathaṃ pratikṣepaṇīyaḥ // 13
children.translated_text: Moreover, in the position that sweet <s>vipāka</s> occurs from a preponderance of earth-moon (water) qualities and pungent from a preponderance of wind-fire-space — when there is a preponderance of mixed qualities, how can the production of the sour, which has a moon-fire (water-fire) nature, be rejected? // 13

children.text: athavā tantrakārayoḥ kim anayor anena vacanamātravirodhena kartavyaṃ yato yadamlapākaṃ carako brūte tatsuśrutena vīryoṣṇam iti kṛtvā samādhīyate tena na kaścid dravyaguṇe virodhaḥ // 14
children.translated_text: Or rather, what concern do the two authors of the treatises (<s>tantrakāras</s>) have with this mere verbal contradiction? Because what <s>Caraka</s> calls 'sour <s>vipāka</s>,' <s>Suśruta</s> reconciles as 'having hot potency (<s>vīrya</s>).' Thus there is no contradiction regarding the properties of substances. // 14

children.text: yattu suśrute'mlapākanirāsārthaṃ dūṣaṇam ucyate pittaṃ hi vidagdhamamlatāmupaiti ityādinā tadanabhyupagamādeva nirastam // 15
children.translated_text: As for the objection stated in <s>Suśruta</s> for the rejection of sour <s>vipāka</s> — 'For <s>Pitta</s>, when corrupted, attains sourness' and so on — that is refuted by the very non-acceptance [of that position by <s>Caraka</s>]. // 15

children.text: nanu lavaṇasya madhurapākitve pittaraktādikartṛtvamanupapannaṃ tathā tiktakaṣāyayoḥ kaṭupākitve pittahantṛtvamanupapannaṃ naivaṃ satyapi lavaṇasya madhurapākitve tatra lavaṇarasa uṣṇaṃ ca vīryaṃ yadasti tena tat pittaraktādikārakaṃ vipākastu tatra pittaraktaharaṇalakṣaṇe kārye bādhitaḥ san sṛṣṭaviṇmūtra ityādinā lakṣaṇena lakṣyata eva // 16
children.translated_text: Now, [one may object]: if salt has sweet <s>vipāka</s>, its production of <s>Pitta</s>, blood disorders, etc. is unjustified. Similarly, if bitter and astringent have pungent <s>vipāka</s>, their <s>Pitta</s>-alleviating nature is unjustified. This is not so, because even when salt has sweet <s>vipāka</s>, the salty <s>rasa</s> and the hot <s>vīrya</s> (potency) that are present in it are what cause <s>Pitta</s>, blood [disorders], etc.; and the <s>vipāka</s> there, though overridden in its <s>Pitta</s>-and-blood-alleviating effect, is still recognizable by the characteristic of facilitating feces and urine, etc. // 16

children.text: etena yaducyate lavaṇe madhuro vipākaścedrasavīryābhyāṃ bādhitaḥ san svakāryakaro na bhavati tatkiṃ tenopadiṣṭeneti tannirastaṃ bhavati // 17
children.translated_text: By this, the objection that 'if salt has sweet <s>vipāka</s>, being overridden by <s>rasa</s> and <s>vīrya</s>, it does not produce its own effect — then what is the point of stating it?' is refuted. // 17

children.text: yato'styeva sṛṣṭaviṇmūtratādinā tatra lavaṇe madhuravipākitvaṃ lakṣaṇīyam // 18
children.translated_text: Because the sweet <s>vipāka</s> nature of salt is indeed recognizable by the facilitation of feces and urine, etc. // 18
By this same approach, the preliminary objections regarding bitter and astringent are also resolved. // 19

children.text: anye tv etaddoṣabhayāl lavaṇo'pyamlaṃ pacyata iti vyākhyānayanti lavaṇastathetyatra tathāśabdena viprakṛṣṭasyāmlamityasya karṣaṇāditi // 20
children.translated_text: Others, however, fearing this difficulty, explain that 'salt too is digested as sour' — [interpreting] the word 'likewise' (<s>tathā</s>) in 'salty likewise' as drawing [the meaning] from the distant [word] 'sour.' // 20

children.text: tanna kaṭvādīnāṃ kaṭurvipāko'mlo'mlasya śeṣayor madhuraḥ iti jatūkarṇavacanāt // 21
children.translated_text: That is incorrect, because of <s>Jatūkarṇa</s>'s statement: 'The <s>vipāka</s> of pungent, etc. is pungent; of sour, sour; and of the remaining two [sweet and salty], sweet.' // 21

children.text: naca vācyaṃ kasmāt traya eva vipākā bhavanti na punastiktādayo'pīti yato bhūtasvabhāva evaiṣaḥ yena madhurādayas traya eva bhavanti bhūtasvabhāvāś cāparyanuyojyāḥ // 22
